# Trellis For TypeScript Consumers

TypeScript-specific usage of Trellis. Read it with [the Trellis guide](llms-core.txt)
from the same Trellis revision, which covers the language-neutral model,
authorization, surfaces, and resources.

## Overview

Trellis requirements concern its own APIs and lifecycle. Configuration parsing,
validation of non-Trellis inputs, databases, DI, code layout, and local testing
tools are application choices. Neither Zod nor an ORM is required.

The npm packages `@oatscenter/trellis` and `@oatscenter/result` contain ESM
JavaScript and TypeScript declarations. Use `import`. CommonJS output and
`require()` support have intentionally been removed, with no compatibility
fallback. Revision 7 targets Node 24 LTS and npm ESM for native TypeScript
tooling, and browser ESM for browser applications. Use ordinary npm dependencies
and Node's standard test runner for native TypeScript tools and tests.

## Generate

Author native IDL, run `trellis update` after dependency changes, and run
`trellis generate` after IDL changes (it re-records your package in
`trellis.lock`). Set `[package]`, `[sources]`, and
`[generate.typescript].output` in `trellis.toml`. For a durable `consumer`,
declare a direct `trellis` source package dependency containing
`trellis.events@v1`; select and lock its version before generation.

Import `apis` and `participants` from that one ordinary local package, for
example `import { participants } from "orders-trellis"` and the generated
participant export. There are no per-API or participant packages. Output is
executable ESM JavaScript plus declarations and `package.json`, at the source
package version, depending on the published runtime matching the CLI. No
consumer transpiler or runtime-path setting is required. Configure ordinary npm
dependencies yourself; generation never edits them. Commit authored files and
the lock, and commit output when ordinary clones should build without the
Trellis CLI or source-package cache. There is no TypeScript contract-authoring
execution step.

Generated types map `int64`/`uint64` to `bigint`, `bytes` to `Uint8Array`, and
the IDL `json` type to `JsonValue` (exported from
`@oatscenter/trellis/generated`); encoding a `json` value rejects anything JSON cannot
represent, such as functions or non-finite numbers.

`timestamp` and `ulid` are branded strings, `Timestamp` and `Ulid`, exported
from `@oatscenter/trellis`. Build them with `timestamp(date?)` (defaults to now)
and `newUlid()`, or parse untrusted strings with `parseTimestamp(value)` and
`parseUlid(value)`, which return `Result<_, ValidationError>`. Timestamps are
normalized to canonical UTC RFC 3339, for example `2026-10-26T02:00:00.5Z`:

```ts
import { newUlid, timestamp } from "@oatscenter/trellis";

await service.publishInvoiceIssued({ id: newUlid(), issuedAt: timestamp() });
```

## Connect

Services import `TrellisService` from `@oatscenter/trellis/service`. Connect
with the generated participant, provisioned identity seed, and Trellis URL;
`name` is optional. Set `telemetry: false` to disable automatic telemetry.
Optional `runtime` controls service logging (including `false` to disable it),
default request timeout, event stream selection, no-responder retry, and health
heartbeat interval. Deployment/instance assignment, installed
package/participant evidence, capabilities, resources, signed session authority,
and transport permissions are resolved server-side; no authorization-context
store or client-supplied deployment/digest fields exist. The complete example is
in `/guides/write-a-service/service-entrypoint`. When the build differs from the
revision its instance runs, `TrellisService.connect` submits the build and
resolves once it installs; a build that asks for new access keeps `connect`
pending until an administrator approves it, logging the review link and printing
it as a QR code on stderr. An administrator's rejection fails `connect`;
`signal` cancels the wait.

When the installation serves a private CA, such as the Trellis-generated
installation CA, start Node services, devices, and native apps with
`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=<path to ca.crt>`. Node then verifies OAuth HTTPS and
native NATS TLS against that CA; never disable certificate verification.

The SDK's shared protocol verifier is a WebAssembly module, fetched as a
separate asset next to the SDK module when a client connects; bundlers that
resolve `new URL(path, import.meta.url)` assets, such as Vite and webpack 5,
need no configuration. In browsers, synchronous protocol helpers such as
`decodeTransferGrant` need a connected client. Services and devices load a
larger provider build automatically through `@oatscenter/trellis/service` and
`@oatscenter/trellis/device`; import that entrypoint before using any other
Trellis API in the process.

Missing live authority is not optional-capability denial. Requests await
verified authority before publication within their original deadline and
cancellation; current authority that excludes the action still denies it.
Requests are never replayed. Signed reply verification waits for
already-received ordered revocation updates before its live checks; it does not
retransmit the request or bypass lost coverage.

### Node native applications

Node native applications import `@oatscenter/trellis/native`, not browser
custody. Use `discoverNativeOAuth`, `NativeOAuthClient.open` with explicit scope
and trust, Device Code or `resume`, and `connectNativeClient` with a generated
native request. For Device Code, show `verificationUriComplete` (the link with
the code filled in; fall back to `verificationUri`) and `userCode` for
comparison. The entrypoint is Node/npm-only and defaults to process-local
memory, with no credential files or SQLite requirement. Retain an explicit
`MemoryNativeOAuthCustody` object to resume the same family across connections
within one process. For remembered login across process restarts, supply an
application-owned `NativeOAuthCustody` provider; Trellis ships no persistent
Node backend. Providers must exclusively acquire the exact family, durably mark
a token spent before returning it for submission, atomically commit successors,
and retain authenticated trust; the SDK awaits those commits.

A successful connection owns the credential family until it closes; an earlier
session reference cannot release that ownership. Await `connection.close()`
before reacquiring: it joins settled exchanges and asynchronous lease release
exactly once, reports release failures, and releases once across repeated
closes.

## Handlers

For a participant declaring RPC `Orders.Create`, with matching generated input
and output models:

```ts
import { Result } from "@oatscenter/trellis";

await service.handleOrdersCreate(({ input }) =>
  Result.ok({ orderId: crypto.randomUUID(), customerId: input.customerId }),
);
```

The UUID is just this example's application identifier. Trellis does not choose
the service's identifier scheme. Register providers, then await
`service.wait()`; stop the service with `service.stop()` during shutdown.

A caller that selects this action calls:

```ts
const order = await client.ordersCreate({ customerId: "customer-1" }).orThrow();
```

Generated flat names depend on action names and alias collisions; inspect the
generated participant when choosing names. There is no `client.rpc.orders.create`
or `service.handle.rpc.orders.create` tree. Dependency selections belong in IDL
`use` blocks, not SDK `use(spec)` calls.

Inline handlers infer their types at registration. Extracted handlers can use
`RpcHandler<typeof participant, "Orders.Create">` from
`@oatscenter/trellis/service`. `OperationHandler`, `LiveHandler`, `JobHandler`,
and `ServiceEventHandler` provide corresponding typed boundaries.
`RpcName<typeof participant>` is the union of owned RPC names, so
`{ [K in RpcName<P>]: RpcHandler<P, K> }` is an exhaustive handler map, and
helpers that receive a handler's `context` take `RpcHandlerContext`. Regenerate
after an IDL change.

Handlers receive Trellis-owned arguments such as `input`, `context`, and the
scoped outbound `client`. Trellis does not inject application dependencies. A
closure is one way to supply a database or domain function; an application can
use its own DI system to construct that closure.

Every public service handler receives the same flat, contract-selected
`ServiceHandlerClient<typeof participant>` as its `client`. It exposes selected
outbound RPC, Operation, Live, and Event-publish methods, owned Event publishers
with `.prepare(...)`, bound `kv`, `store`, and `jobs` handles,
`connection`/`name`, and `availability()`, `watchAvailability()`,
`publishPrepared(...)`, and `transfer(...)`. Registration and lifecycle methods
stay on the connected service; there is no generic
`client.rpc`/`client.operation`/`client.event` tree.

Declare wire models and expected errors in IDL. The generator owns the runtime
schemas and generated error types. Construct a declared error from its declared
payload alone, `new OrderNotFound({ orderId })` (or `new Gone()` without one);
an optional second argument sets `message` (default: the error name),
`context`, or `cause`, while `id`, `type` and the trace ID are filled in.
`error.payload` holds the declared fields. Handlers return declared errors
through `Result.err(...)`; callers can distinguish them from runtime/transport
failures.
`.orThrow()` converts a failed result to an exception where that matches the
application's control flow. Native cursor-paginated RPCs add lazy `.pages()` and
`.items()` iterators.

RPC `RequestOpts.signal` cancels the caller's wait with
`trellis.request.cancelled`, including after publication; an elapsed deadline
reports `trellis.request.timeout`. Neither undoes accepted work.
`TransportError` code `trellis.request.unavailable` with `noResponders: true`
means the target service is not responding; restore reachability and retry
observation of the same work rather than starting replacement business work.

## Events And Live

For a declared event `Orders.Changed`, generated service methods include
`publishOrdersChanged(...)` and, when selected, `onOrdersChanged(...)`:

```ts
await service
  .onOrdersChanged(({ event }) => {
    console.log(event);
    return Result.ok(undefined);
  })
  .orThrow();
```

The `event` is the typed payload; `context` carries runtime metadata. Durable
delivery comes from declared Consumer resources. The runtime owns durable
identity, local concurrency, retry, proof verification, and the scoped Events
DLQ.

Live providers receive an abort signal. Stop connection-scoped work when it
aborts, and close or abort a caller subscription when no longer needed. A caller
subscription is an owned async iterator: call `return()`/`throw()` or abort its
signal to release it; disposal is idempotent even before the first `next()`.

## Operations

For operation `Reports.Generate`:

```ts
const operation = await client.reportsGenerate(input).start().orThrow();
const terminal = await operation.wait().orThrow();
if (terminal.state === "completed") console.log(terminal.output);
```

The provider registers through its generated participant facade. Open a watcher
before reading the current snapshot. Transfer-capable invocations return a
transfer-aware result; consult its generated type rather than assuming the
ordinary operation result shape.

In a handler, `op.ref` is the operation's complete serialized reference; a
caller restores it with `client.reportsGenerate.resume(ref)`.

The generated `service.handleReportsGenerate.control(id)` returns a typed
owner-fenced local handle; non-owners cannot borrow the fence. Use
`service.handleReportsGenerate.reconcile(id)` from another replica to ask the
current owner to re-enter the handler. The handler's `signal` aborts on
cancellation or ownership loss; await cleanup of side-effecting children before
returning. Caller `operation.cancel()` returns terminal `Cancelled` only after
this cleanup and the fenced terminal write. Throwing, returning an error, or
`op.defer()` does not acknowledge successful cleanup. Recovered handlers enter
with the signal already aborted: check it and clean up before business work, and
return successfully only after cleanup completes. A stale executor cannot
finalize cancellation.

Starts default to canonical routing. For explicit pre-acceptance ownership,
persist deployment, invocation ULID, and frozen input before sending, then use
`.start(undefined, { invocationId, targetDeploymentId })`. Cancellation-first
admission adds `cancellationRequested: true` with a caller-chosen ULID and the
same frozen input on every retry. Native cancellation-first admission also
supports upload operations without opening upload staging, so handler `transfer`
is optional: handle already-aborted cleanup before accessing it, and require a
transfer handle on the ordinary upload branch. The transfer-start builder
accepts the target and invocation ID but not cancellation-first, because its
result describes an actual transfer.

### Transfers

For upload Operations, use the generated `.transfer(body).start()` workflow.
Upload bodies accept `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` and `AsyncIterable<Uint8Array>`.
The runtime snapshots bounded blocks before advancing an iterator, so a producer
may reuse a scratch buffer between chunks. `Uint8Array`/`ArrayBuffer` bodies
remain caller-owned and must stay unchanged until upload settlement; bounded SDK
queues do not bound producer-provided backing buffers. The provider consumes
runtime-staged bytes with `transfer.stream()` or `transfer.bytes()`. Web Streams
backpressure drives cumulative credit. The connection `timeout` covers transfer
activation from transport acquisition through the provider reply, and separately
bounds cancellation; it is not a body lifetime limit. A cancellation timeout
releases local ownership but does not confirm remote cleanup.

For `stream;` Operations, callers use the same `.transfer(body).start()`. The
handler starts immediately; `transfer.stream()` returns the caller's live bytes
exactly once (a second call fails), and `transfer.completed()` resolves after
verified delivery. Serve generated downloads with
`service.createTransfer({ direction: "receive", stream, info, context })`,
where `context` is the RPC handler's context (the grant is bound to its verified
caller and permission) and `info` declares the exact size and `SHA-256=` digest.

For a download RPC's untrusted `transfer` field, call
`decodeTransferGrant(response.transfer).orThrow()` from `@oatscenter/trellis`,
check `grant.direction === "receive"`, and pass the decoded grant to
`client.transfer(grant)`. Receive grants use the helper's `stream()` for large
bodies or `bytes()` for a collected buffer.

## Jobs

Private queues are available as `service.jobs.<queue>`. Register handlers with
`handle(...)`, create work with `create(...)`, and observe the returned job
reference. Retry and automatic delivery acknowledgement are runtime-owned.
Worker concurrency is local; optional keyed concurrency is a declared semantic
policy. Before business work, check `job.signal.aborted`: already-aborted job
handlers must reconcile earlier side effects. A recovered owner after
fail-stale takeover sees `job.signal.reason === "stale-attempt"`.

## Resources

Use generated State, KV, Store, Consumer, and Job handles. These are
Trellis-managed handles, not an application database abstraction.

Retain `const state = client.state.savedResource` for app State. Generated
schemas register before the first operation at expected revision "0"; explicitly
`await state.register("0")` to retain its Result containing the registration
revision. Representation changes require
`state.register(currentRegistrationRevision, idempotencyKey)`.
`const observation = (await state.watch()).orThrow()` opens certified Live Watch;
use `for await (const snapshot of observation)` for the initial snapshot and
updates, where undefined means unwritten or deleted. Leaving iteration or
`observation.close()` releases it, and `observation.closed` reports the Live
terminal outcome.

Use Store entry `stream()` for large bodies; `bytes()` consumes the same reader
but retains the entire object in memory. Streams fail on physical disconnect or
closure. `TypedStore.list(...)` and file metadata lists use the shared keyset
pagination.

### SQL outbox

When SQL writes and event/job intents need one atomic commit, configure
`service.createSqlOutbox(...)` with `dialect`, an `executor`, and a
`transaction` runner. The transaction runner supplies the application's `tx` and
a transaction-scoped `SqlExecutor`:

```ts
await outbox
  .transaction(async ({ tx, event, job }) => {
    await orders.markShipped(tx, orderId);
    await event.orders.shipped.enqueue({ orderId }).orThrow();
  })
  .orThrow();
```

Here `orders` and `tx` belong to the application. The transaction-scoped event
tree is an outbox API, unlike ordinary flat publish methods; normal event
facades do not expose `enqueue`. Job submission intents use the callback's `job`
tree. `getSqlOutboxMigrations(...)` returns Trellis helper-table migration
artifacts for the application's migration tool to apply.

Applications adapt their chosen database and transaction handles to the generic
`SqlExecutor` interface; Trellis does not provide ORM-specific adapters.
`claimDue(...)` returns the claimed records; pass a record, not just its ID, to
`markDispatched(...)` or `markFailed(...)`, which return false when a newer
claim superseded it. KV acquisition and completion use revision CAS. SQL inbox
`record()` returns true only for the call that inserted the ID; commit that
marker with a domain side effect when both must be atomic.

## Browser Apps

Browser apps use `TrellisClient.connect({ request, trellisUrl, auth: {
clientId, redirectTo } })` with a generated browser request descriptor, or the
[Svelte integration](llms-svelte.txt). A new app may identify itself by an HTTPS
CIMD document; it does not require administrator registration.

The SDK owns PKCE, DPoP, IndexedDB custody, exact callback validation, authority
renewal, and transport maintenance. Persistent DPoP and encryption keys stay
nonextractable in IndexedDB, and refresh exchange and commit share a Web Lock
across tabs. A lost refresh response marks recovery required instead of
replaying a spent token; credential handles cannot silently switch to another
principal, and refresh-successor checkpointing is restricted to actual refresh
exchanges. Retained clients refresh discovery from durable cross-tab trust
before consuming a refresh token, with no client recreation or page reload.
Browser IndexedDB version 3 persists only the initiating session seed, nullable
login metadata, pending signed intent/intent ID, and generation tombstone, keyed
by canonical origin plus stable participant ID; compare-and-swap fences prevent
stale tabs from overwriting newer state.

`onAuthRequired` receives `loginUrl` and `mode: "browser"`; caller-owned
navigation may return `{ status: "handled" }`. Use the connected client's
`logout()` to revoke its OAuth family and close its connection while retaining
the Portal login. Never fabricate OAuth or authority metadata in application
callbacks. Coverage loss suspends application use without invalidating retained
identity; a cancelled renewal settles before its replacement starts, and logical
close cancels maintenance and renewal.

## Devices

Pass the companion's independently held session as
`TrellisDevice.connect({ ..., companion: { session, servers } })`. Obtain it by
declaring Auth's `deviceCompanionsManage` in the child request, completing
ordinary explicit OAuth user consent, and calling `DeviceCompanions.Attach` from
that verified user connection with the approved review; then close that setup
connection and resume its native credential handle. The wrapper checks signed
request/client/grant assignment.

## Accounts

Generated account calls follow the language-neutral rules. Use
`user.account.profileRevision` as `expectedRevision` for `usersProfileUpdate`
with a fresh idempotency key. Administrative `usersUpdate` uses lifecycle
`expectedRevision`; omit unchanged profile fields for lifecycle-only saves, and
add `expectedProfileRevision` for intentional profile edits. Both revisions are
checked atomically.

## Testing

For live Node tests, `await using runtime = await TrellisTestRuntime.start()`
from `@oatscenter/trellis-testkit` downloads the latest Trellis CLI/server
release (newest stable, else newest prerelease; `TRELLIS_TEST_VERSION` selects
another), verified against its published checksum, currently for Linux x86-64
only; no installed Trellis executables or nsc are required. Use
`trellis: { source: { kind: "path", cli, server } }`, or set both
`TRELLIS_TEST_CLI_BIN` and `TRELLIS_TEST_SERVER_BIN`, for a prebuilt pair, with
no fallback. `restart()` retains data and identity and
restarts the full host and broker. Stop first requests graceful host shutdown;
on timeout or host exit, isolated process-group cleanup reclaims remaining owned
children before sandbox removal. Startup requires `/readyz` metadata's
`processId` to match the spawned native host. `firstAdmin: "browser-flow"` opts
into browser setup.

The kit adds each runtime's CA (`runtime.caCertificate`) to the test process's
Node trust, so SDK clients need no TLS options. Launch Playwright browsers with
`env: browserTrustEnvironment()`, which builds a private NSS trust store holding
those CAs (requires NSS `certutil`); never use `ignoreHTTPSErrors`. Pass
`NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=runtime.caCertificate` to spawned Node processes and
`--ca-certificate runtime.caCertificate` (or `--ca-fingerprint` with its
SHA-256 fingerprint) to `trellis login`.

Live testkit users are ordinary accounts: `runtime.createUser({ name })`, then
`runtime.grantUserCapabilities({ user, capabilityIds })`, then
`runtime.connectClient({ name, contract, user })` (or `registerClient`).
Omitting `user` retains the seeded-admin helper. Use generated participants
rather than handwritten bootstrap responses; see
`/guides/testing-trellis-services`. Regenerate SDKs, then run the repository's
own checks.
